stimuli.title: Six persons on a bench, with distances
stimuli.content:
Six persons Gitanjali, Hridaan, Ishwari, Jasleen, Keshav and Lakshya sit on a long straight bench, all facing north. The gaps between neighbours are not all equal; distances are measured along the bench.

- Jasleen sits at the extreme left end of the bench.
- Keshav sits 7 m to the right of Jasleen, and exactly one person sits between them.
- Hridaan sits 3 m to the left of Keshav.
- Ishwari sits at the extreme right end of the bench, 13 m to the right of Keshav.
- Gitanjali sits 8 m to the left of Ishwari.
- Lakshya sits 2 m away from Gitanjali but not between Keshav and Gitanjali.
stimuli.solution:
Measure every position in metres east of Jasleen (the left end). Keshav = 7, and the one person between them is Hridaan at 7 − 3 = 4. Ishwari = 7 + 13 = 20 (the right end) and Gitanjali = 20 − 8 = 12. Lakshya is 2 m from Gitanjali: 10 lies between Keshav (7) and Gitanjali (12), so Lakshya = 14.

| Person | Metres east of Jasleen |
|---|---|
| Jasleen | 0 |
| Hridaan | 4 |
| Keshav | 7 |
| Gitanjali | 12 |
| Lakshya | 14 |
| Ishwari | 20 |

stimuli.title: Six friends at a hexagonal table, with drinks
stimuli.content:
Six friends Bhavesh, Chaitali, Dhaval, Eesha, Faraz and Hemlata sit around a hexagonal table, one at each side, all facing the centre. Each of them drinks a different one of Coffee, Juice, Lassi, Milk, Soup and Tea. (Facing the centre, a person's right is anticlockwise.)

- Dhaval sits opposite Bhavesh.
- Eesha sits immediately to the right of Bhavesh.
- Chaitali sits second to the right of Dhaval.
- Faraz sits immediately to the left of Chaitali.
- Bhavesh drinks Tea, and the person who drinks Coffee sits opposite him.
- The person who drinks Milk sits between Eesha and Dhaval.
- The person who drinks Lassi sits immediately to the right of the person who drinks Soup.
stimuli.solution:
Fix Bhavesh. Dhaval is opposite him, Eesha immediately to his right, Chaitali two places to Dhaval's right (immediately to Bhavesh's left) and Faraz between Dhaval and Chaitali. Hemlata takes the seat between Eesha and Dhaval. Bhavesh drinks Tea and Dhaval, opposite him, Coffee. The Milk drinker sits between Eesha and Dhaval: Hemlata. Of Eesha, Faraz and Chaitali, the only Soup–Lassi pair with Lassi immediately to the right is Faraz (Soup) and Chaitali (Lassi), so Eesha drinks Juice.

| Seat (anticlockwise from Bhavesh) | Person | Drink |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Bhavesh | Tea |
| 1 | Eesha | Juice |
| 2 | Hemlata | Milk |
| 3 | Dhaval | Coffee |
| 4 | Faraz | Soup |
| 5 | Chaitali | Lassi |

stimuli.title: Eight persons at a square table, all facing the centre
stimuli.content:
Eight persons Kashish, Lalitha, Mukund, Neelam, Oorvi, Parveen, Raghu and Sanjana sit around a square table, all facing the centre. Four of them sit at the four corners and the other four at the middle of the four sides, so corner and middle seats alternate around the table.

- Kashish sits at one of the corners.
- Mukund sits opposite Kashish.
- Neelam sits second to the right of Kashish.
- Sanjana sits between Neelam and Mukund.
- Lalitha sits immediately to the left of Kashish.
- Parveen sits at a corner.
- Oorvi is not an immediate neighbour of Kashish.
stimuli.solution:
Fix Kashish at a corner. Mukund is opposite her (also a corner) and Neelam two seats to her right (a corner). Sanjana sits between Neelam and Mukund, and Lalitha immediately to Kashish's left (a middle seat). The seats left are the middle seat to Kashish's right, the middle seat after Mukund and the corner after it. Parveen takes the corner. Oorvi cannot be next to Kashish, so Oorvi takes the middle seat after Mukund and Raghu the middle seat to Kashish's right.

| Seat (anticlockwise from Kashish) | Person | Position |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Kashish | corner |
| 1 | Raghu | middle of a side |
| 2 | Neelam | corner |
| 3 | Sanjana | middle of a side |
| 4 | Mukund | corner |
| 5 | Oorvi | middle of a side |
| 6 | Parveen | corner |
| 7 | Lalitha | middle of a side |

stimuli.title: Eight persons around a circle, with ages and mixed facing
stimuli.content:
Eight persons Anvesha, Bhairav, Chandrika, Dilnawaz, Evan, Ginni, Hussain and Ilina sit around a circular table, equally spaced. Some of them face the centre and the others face outside. (For a person facing the centre the right is anticlockwise; for a person facing outside the right is clockwise.) Their ages are 22, 26, 31, 35, 40, 44, 49 and 53 years, one age each.

- Anvesha faces the centre, and Bhairav sits opposite her.
- Chandrika faces the centre and sits second to the right of Anvesha.
- Hussain, the youngest of the eight, sits between Anvesha and Chandrika and faces outside.
- Evan sits immediately to the right of Chandrika.
- Ilina sits second to the left of Evan.
- Dilnawaz sits immediately to the right of Ilina.
- Bhairav is 4 years older than Hussain.
- The oldest person sits second to the right of Anvesha.
- Only two persons are older than Ilina.
- Ginni is older than Anvesha.
- Evan is younger than Dilnawaz, and Dilnawaz is younger than Anvesha.
- Exactly four persons face the centre.
- Dilnawaz and Ginni face the same direction.
stimuli.solution:
Fix Anvesha (facing the centre); Bhairav is opposite her and Chandrika two seats anticlockwise, with Hussain (22, facing outside) between them. Chandrika faces the centre, so Evan is the next seat anticlockwise. If Evan faced the centre, second to his left (clockwise) would be Chandrika's seat, so Evan faces outside and Ilina sits two seats anticlockwise from him, next to Bhairav. If Ilina faced outside, the seat to her right would be Bhairav's, so Ilina faces the centre and Dilnawaz sits next to her; Ginni takes the last seat, beside Anvesha. Anvesha, Chandrika and Ilina face the centre; exactly one more does, and Dilnawaz and Ginni face the same way, so both face outside and Bhairav faces the centre. Ages: Bhairav 26, Chandrika (second to Anvesha's right) 53, Ilina 44. Ginni, Anvesha, Dilnawaz and Evan share 31, 35, 40 and 49 with Ginni > Anvesha > Dilnawaz > Evan.

| Seat (anticlockwise from Anvesha) | Person | Faces | Age |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | Anvesha | centre | 40 |
| 1 | Hussain | outside | 22 |
| 2 | Chandrika | centre | 53 |
| 3 | Evan | outside | 31 |
| 4 | Bhairav | centre | 26 |
| 5 | Ilina | centre | 44 |
| 6 | Dilnawaz | outside | 35 |
| 7 | Ginni | outside | 49 |

stimuli.title: A circle of unknown size
stimuli.content:
Some persons sit around a circular table, equally spaced and all facing the centre. The number of persons is not given. Jharna, Kuber, Lajwanti, Mrinal, Nishit and Paromita are among them; the others are not named.

- Kuber sits third to the right of Jharna.
- Only five persons sit between Jharna and Kuber when counted to the left of Jharna.
- Lajwanti sits second to the left of Kuber.
- Only two persons sit between Mrinal and Kuber.
- Nishit sits immediately to the left of Jharna.
- Paromita sits immediately to the right of Kuber.
stimuli.solution:
Count positions anticlockwise (to the right) from Jharna = 0. Kuber = 3, with two persons between them on Jharna's right. Five persons sit between them on Jharna's left, so the circle has 2 + 5 + 2 = 9 persons. Lajwanti = 3 − 2 = 1, Paromita = 4 and Nishit = 8 (immediately to Jharna's left). Mrinal is three places from Kuber: 6 or 0; 0 is Jharna, so Mrinal = 6. Positions 2, 5 and 7 hold unnamed persons.

| Position (anticlockwise from Jharna) | Person |
|---|---|
| 0 | Jharna |
| 1 | Lajwanti |
| 2 | an unnamed person |
| 3 | Kuber |
| 4 | Paromita |
| 5 | an unnamed person |
| 6 | Mrinal |
| 7 | an unnamed person |
| 8 | Nishit |

stimuli.title: Seven persons from the ground floor up
stimuli.content:
Seven persons Bilal, Chhaya, Damodar, Esther, Gurleen, Harsha and Jeevika live in a building that has a ground floor and six floors above it. The ground floor is numbered 0 and the topmost floor 6; one person lives on each floor. Each person works in a different city among Agra, Bhopal, Kochi, Nagpur, Patna, Surat and Thane.

- Damodar lives on floor 3 and works in Patna.
- Only two persons live between Damodar and the person who works in Kochi, who lives above Damodar.
- Esther works in Kochi.
- Harsha lives on the ground floor.
- The person who works in Surat lives immediately below Esther.
- Bilal and Chhaya live on odd-numbered floors, and Bilal lives above Chhaya.
- Gurleen lives immediately above the person who works in Bhopal.
- The person who works in Thane lives between Chhaya and Damodar.
- Jeevika does not work in Nagpur.
stimuli.solution:
Damodar = 3 (Patna); the Kochi worker, Esther, lives three floors higher: 6. The Surat worker lives on floor 5. Harsha = 0. Bilal and Chhaya take odd floors other than 3 with Bilal higher: Bilal = 5 (Surat) and Chhaya = 1. Floors 2 and 4 remain for Gurleen and Jeevika. Gurleen is immediately above the Bhopal worker: Gurleen = 4 would make Damodar (Patna) the Bhopal worker, so Gurleen = 2, Chhaya works in Bhopal and Jeevika = 4. The Thane worker lives between Chhaya (1) and Damodar (3): Gurleen. Jeevika does not work in Nagpur, so Jeevika works in Agra and Harsha in Nagpur.

| Floor | Person | City |
|---|---|---|
| 6 | Esther | Kochi |
| 5 | Bilal | Surat |
| 4 | Jeevika | Agra |
| 3 | Damodar | Patna |
| 2 | Gurleen | Thane |
| 1 | Chhaya | Bhopal |
| 0 | Harsha | Nagpur |

stimuli.title: Eight persons, two on each of four floors
stimuli.content:
Eight persons Kavita, Manish, Natasha, Pallav, Ronak, Shalini, Uttam and Vibha live in a four-storey building, two persons on each floor. Floor 1 is the lowermost and floor 4 the topmost.

- Kavita lives on an odd-numbered floor, and Ronak lives on the floor immediately below Kavita's floor.
- Manish lives on the topmost floor.
- Natasha lives on the same floor as Ronak.
- Pallav lives on a floor below Natasha's floor.
- Shalini lives neither on Kavita's floor nor on Manish's floor.
- Uttam lives on a floor above Shalini's floor but below Vibha's floor.
- Exactly two persons live on each floor.
stimuli.solution:
Kavita is on an odd floor with Ronak one floor below, so Kavita = 3 and Ronak = 2 (Kavita = 1 leaves no floor below). Manish = 4. Natasha joins Ronak on floor 2, which is now full, and Pallav lives below it: floor 1. Shalini avoids floors 3 and 4, so she is on floor 1. Uttam lives between Shalini and Vibha: one place is left on floor 3 and one on floor 4, so Uttam = 3 and Vibha = 4.

| Floor | Persons |
|---|---|
| 4 | Manish and Vibha |
| 3 | Kavita and Uttam |
| 2 | Natasha and Ronak |
| 1 | Pallav and Shalini |

stimuli.title: A building of unknown height
stimuli.content:
Some persons live in a building, one person on each floor; every floor is occupied. Floor 1 is the lowermost. The number of floors is not given. Aarush, Bhoomika, Chakor, Devika, Ekansh and Fiona live in the building; the other residents are not named.

- Chakor lives on floor 4.
- Only three persons live between Chakor and Devika, and Devika lives above Chakor.
- Aarush lives on the topmost floor, and only five persons live between Aarush and Devika.
- Ekansh lives exactly midway between Chakor and Aarush.
- Fiona lives as many floors below Chakor as Ekansh lives above Devika.
- Only two persons live between Bhoomika and Aarush.
stimuli.solution:
Chakor = 4, so Devika = 8. Aarush is six floors from Devika and lives on the top floor, so Aarush = 14 (2 is below Devika and cannot be the top): the building has 14 floors. Ekansh = (4 + 14) ÷ 2 = 9, one floor above Devika, so Fiona is one floor below Chakor: 3. Bhoomika is three floors from Aarush: 11.

| Floor | Person |
|---|---|
| 14 | Aarush |
| 11 | Bhoomika |
| 9 | Ekansh |
| 8 | Devika |
| 4 | Chakor |
| 3 | Fiona |

stimuli.title: Nine boxes in three stacks
stimuli.content:
Nine boxes B, D, G, K, M, P, S, V and X are kept in three stacks, left, middle and right, with three boxes in each stack. Level 1 is the bottom of a stack and level 3 its top.

- Box V is at level 2 of the middle stack.
- Box D is placed directly above box V.
- Box K is at the bottom of the stack that holds box D.
- Box G is at the bottom of the right stack.
- Box P is at the same level as box V but not in the same stack as box B.
- Box B is placed directly below box X.
- Box S is at the bottom of its stack.
- Box S is not in the same stack as box M.
stimuli.solution:
Middle stack: K (bottom), V, D. G is at the bottom of the right stack, so S, also at a bottom, is at the bottom of the left stack. P is at level 2 of the left or right stack. If P were in the left stack, B (not in P's stack) would have to be in the right stack with X above it: B at level 2, X at level 3; then M would join S in the left stack, which is not allowed. So P is at level 2 of the right stack, B and X fill levels 2 and 3 of the left stack, and M tops the right stack.

| Level | Left | Middle | Right |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | X | D | M |
| 2 | B | V | P |
| 1 | S | K | G |

stimuli.title: Eight boxes in four colours
stimuli.content:
Eight boxes C, E, H, J, L, N, R and T are kept one above another in a single stack (position 1 is the bottom, 8 the top). Each box is Blue, Green, Red or White, and exactly two boxes are of each colour.

- Box T is placed fourth from the bottom and is blue.
- The other blue box is at the top of the stack.
- Each green box is placed immediately below a blue box.
- Box L is placed immediately above box T.
- Box C is green and is placed above box L.
- Box J is at the bottom and is red.
- Exactly two boxes are placed between the two white boxes.
- Box E is green.
- Box N is placed below box R, and box H is blue.
stimuli.solution:
Blue boxes: T (4) and the top box (8). The green boxes sit just below them: positions 3 and 7. L = 5. C is green and above L, so C = 7; E, the other green box, = 3. J = 1 (red). Positions 2, 5 and 6 hold one red and two white boxes; the whites have two boxes between them, so they are at 2 and 5 and position 6 is red. H is blue, so H = 8; N below R puts N at 2 and R at 6.

| Position | Box | Colour |
|---|---|---|
| 8 | H | Blue |
| 7 | C | Green |
| 6 | R | Red |
| 5 | L | White |
| 4 | T | Blue |
| 3 | E | Green |
| 2 | N | White |
| 1 | J | Red |

stimuli.title: Seven workshops from April to October, with colours
stimuli.content:
Seven persons Anaya, Bodhi, Chinmayi, Daivik, Eila, Girik and Hiral attend a workshop, one person in each month from April to October of the same year. Each of them likes a different colour among Blue, Green, Maroon, Orange, Pink, White and Yellow.

- Chinmayi's workshop is in a month that has 31 days, and only two workshops are held after hers.
- The person who likes White attends two months before Chinmayi.
- Girik attends in the month immediately after the person who likes White.
- Eila attends in the month immediately after Chinmayi, and Bodhi attends after Eila.
- Daivik attends before Hiral, and neither of them likes White.
- The person who likes Maroon attends in the last month.
- Chinmayi likes Green, and the person who likes Yellow attends immediately before her.
- Hiral likes neither Pink nor Orange, and Eila does not like Pink.
stimuli.solution:
Two workshops come after Chinmayi's, so hers is in August (31 days). White is two months earlier: June; Girik follows in July. Eila is in September and Bodhi, after her, in October. April, May and June remain for Anaya, Daivik and Hiral; Daivik and Hiral do not like White, so Anaya is in June and Daivik (April) is before Hiral (May). Chinmayi likes Green and Girik (July) Yellow; Bodhi (October) likes Maroon. Blue, Orange and Pink remain for Daivik, Hiral and Eila: Hiral takes Blue, and Eila, not Pink, takes Orange; Daivik likes Pink.

| Month | Person | Colour |
|---|---|---|
| April | Daivik | Pink |
| May | Hiral | Blue |
| June | Anaya | White |
| July | Girik | Yellow |
| August | Chinmayi | Green |
| September | Eila | Orange |
| October | Bodhi | Maroon |

stimuli.title: Six appointments in a month that starts on a Monday
stimuli.content:
Six customers Nirmal, Oishi, Pavan, Rasika, Shubh and Vedika each have one appointment at a bank in the same month, on six different dates. The month has 30 days, and its 1st is a Monday.

- Oishi's appointment is on the second Wednesday of the month.
- Nirmal's appointment is exactly one week before Oishi's.
- Shubh's appointment is on the fourth Monday of the month.
- Rasika's appointment is on a Friday before Shubh's.
- Pavan's appointment is on a Sunday, after Oishi's but before Rasika's.
- Vedika's appointment is on the last Saturday of the month.
stimuli.solution:
Mondays fall on 1, 8, 15, 22, 29; Wednesdays on 3, 10, 17, 24; Fridays on 5, 12, 19, 26; Saturdays on 6, 13, 20, 27; Sundays on 7, 14, 21, 28. Oishi = 10 (second Wednesday), Nirmal = 3, Shubh = 22 (fourth Monday), Vedika = 27 (last Saturday). Rasika is on a Friday before the 22nd: 5, 12 or 19, and a Sunday (Pavan) must fit between the 10th and Rasika's date, so Rasika = 19 and Pavan = 14.

| Customer | Date | Day |
|---|---|---|
| Nirmal | 3 | Wednesday |
| Oishi | 10 | Wednesday |
| Pavan | 14 | Sunday |
| Rasika | 19 | Friday |
| Shubh | 22 | Monday |
| Vedika | 27 | Saturday |

stimuli.title: Eight officers joining over two years
stimuli.content:
Eight officers Aadya, Bhavin, Darpan, Eshwari, Gyan, Hetal, Jagrut and Kirtana joined a bank. Each joined in a different one of these eight months: March, June, September and December of 2024, and March, June, September and December of 2025.

- Bhavin joined in June of one of the two years.
- Only three persons joined between Bhavin and Darpan, and Darpan joined before Bhavin.
- Aadya joined in December of the year in which Darpan joined.
- Eshwari joined immediately after Bhavin, and Gyan joined after Eshwari.
- Hetal joined before Kirtana, and both of them joined in the same year.
stimuli.solution:
List the eight months in time order (Mar 24, Jun 24, Sep 24, Dec 24, Mar 25, Jun 25, Sep 25, Dec 25). Bhavin joined in a June and Darpan four places earlier, so Bhavin = June 2025 and Darpan = June 2024. Aadya = December 2024. Eshwari = September 2025 and Gyan, after her, = December 2025. March 2024, September 2024 and March 2025 remain; Hetal and Kirtana joined in the same year with Hetal first, so Hetal = March 2024, Kirtana = September 2024 and Jagrut = March 2025.

| Month | Officer |
|---|---|
| March 2024 | Hetal |
| June 2024 | Darpan |
| September 2024 | Kirtana |
| December 2024 | Aadya |
| March 2025 | Jagrut |
| June 2025 | Bhavin |
| September 2025 | Eshwari |
| December 2025 | Gyan |

stimuli.title: Seven hobby classes in a week
stimuli.content:
Seven persons Abeer, Brinda, Darius, Elora, Gauransh, Ivaan and Mehr each attend one hobby class in the same week, one class on each day from Monday to Sunday. The classes are Chess, Cooking, Dance, Music, Painting, Pottery and Yoga, one each.

- Mehr's class is exactly in the middle of the week.
- Only two classes are held between Mehr's class and the Cooking class, which is held after Mehr's.
- The Dance class is held on Friday.
- Abeer attends the Music class, which is held two days before the Dance class.
- Elora attends on Monday, and Gauransh attends the Chess class.
- Darius attends on the day immediately before Brinda.
- Ivaan attends after Darius, but not on Saturday.
- Mehr attends neither Painting nor Yoga, and Brinda does not attend Yoga.
stimuli.solution:
Mehr = Thursday, Cooking = Sunday, Dance = Friday, and Music (Abeer) = Wednesday. Elora = Monday. Tuesday, Friday, Saturday and Sunday remain for Brinda, Darius, Gauransh and Ivaan. Darius–Brinda are consecutive: Friday–Saturday (Saturday–Sunday would leave no later day for Ivaan). Ivaan = Sunday (Cooking) and Gauransh = Tuesday (Chess); Darius takes Dance. Of Painting, Pottery and Yoga, Mehr takes Pottery, Brinda Painting and Elora Yoga.

| Day | Person | Class |
|---|---|---|
| Monday | Elora | Yoga |

stimuli.title: Six officers, designations and postings
stimuli.content:
Six officers Nikunj, Quresh, Rutvi, Saanvi, Tanush and Udit hold six different designations. In decreasing order of seniority the designations are: Director, Joint Director, Deputy Director, Assistant Director, Section Officer and Assistant. Each officer is posted in a different city among Indore, Jaipur, Lucknow, Mysuru, Ranchi and Shimla.

- Only two officers are senior to Nikunj.
- The officer posted in Jaipur is immediately junior to Nikunj, and Saanvi is posted in Jaipur.
- Tanush is junior to Quresh, who is junior to Saanvi.
- Rutvi is senior to Udit.
- The officer posted in Shimla is senior to the officer posted in Indore, and both are senior to Nikunj.
- The Assistant is posted in Lucknow.
- Quresh is not posted in Ranchi.
stimuli.solution:
Nikunj is third (Deputy Director) and Saanvi fourth (Assistant Director, Jaipur). Quresh and Tanush are junior to Saanvi: Section Officer and Assistant, in that order. Rutvi (Director) is senior to Udit (Joint Director). The Shimla and Indore officers are the two above Nikunj, Shimla first: Rutvi – Shimla, Udit – Indore. Tanush (Assistant) is in Lucknow. Mysuru and Ranchi remain for Nikunj and Quresh; Quresh is not in Ranchi, so Quresh – Mysuru and Nikunj – Ranchi.

stimuli.title: Coding by word length, then vowels
stimuli.content:
In a certain code language, each word is coded by the steps below.
Step 1: If the word has an even number of letters, its first half and second half are interchanged. If the word has an odd number of letters, its middle letter is replaced by the number of letters in the word.
Step 2: Every vowel (A, E, I, O, U) in the result of Step 1 is replaced by the letter that comes immediately after it in the English alphabet.

Each question gives a word; choose its code.
stimuli.solution: Count the letters first (even: swap the halves; odd: replace the middle letter by the count), then move every remaining vowel one step forward. Consonants and the inserted number do not change in Step 2.

stimuli.title: Seeds that farmers keep
stimuli.content:
In many Indian villages, farmers once kept a portion of every harvest aside as seed for the next season. Grandmothers stored grain in earthen pots sealed with mud and ash, and families exchanged seeds at weddings and fairs. Over time, this practice faded. High-yielding hybrid seeds, sold in bright packets in the market town, promised bigger harvests, and many farmers stopped saving their own.

The new seeds did raise yields, especially where water and fertiliser were plentiful. But they came with a catch. Hybrid seeds do not breed true, so a farmer who saves them finds that the next crop is weaker and uneven. He must therefore buy fresh seed every year, often on credit, and the cost rises with each season. In a dry year, when the crop fails, the farmer is left with a loan and nothing to show for it.

Community seed banks are an attempt to bring back the old habit in an organised form. A group of farmers, often led by women, collects seeds of local varieties, cleans and dries them, and stores them in a common room. A member who borrows a kilogram of seed at sowing time returns two kilograms after the harvest, so the stock grows from year to year. Records are kept in a simple register, and the seeds are tested for germination before they are lent.

The local varieties held in these banks may not match hybrids in a good year, but many of them tolerate drought, pests and poor soil far better. For a small farmer who cannot afford irrigation, a crop that yields a little less but rarely fails completely can be the wiser choice. Seed banks also preserve varieties that might otherwise disappear forever, along with the knowledge of how to grow and cook them.

Seed banks are not a rejection of modern science. Several of them work with agricultural universities to improve local varieties without losing their toughness. Their real value lies in giving farmers a choice: to buy seed when it suits them, and to rely on their own when it does not.

stimuli.title: Pumps that run on sunshine
stimuli.content:
For decades, farmers in many parts of India have watered their fields with pumps run on diesel or on grid electricity. Diesel is expensive and its price keeps changing, while the power supplied to farms often arrives for only a few hours a day, sometimes in the middle of the night. A farmer may have to walk to his field at two in the morning simply because that is when the current comes.

Solar pumps offer a way out of this daily struggle. Panels set up beside the field run the pump during daylight, when the farmer is already at work, and the fuel, sunlight, costs nothing. Once the pump is installed, the cost of running it is very low, and there is no smoke or noise. Government schemes now meet a large part of the purchase price, which has brought these pumps within the reach of many small farmers.

The benefits, however, come with a risk. Because water from a solar pump is almost free, a farmer has little reason to use it carefully. In areas where groundwater levels are already falling, free pumping could drain aquifers even faster, leaving everyone with deeper and drier wells. Experts therefore suggest that solar pumps should be combined with drip irrigation, which delivers water directly to the roots of plants and wastes very little.

Another idea being tried in some states is to connect solar pumps to the electricity grid. On days when the farmer does not need to irrigate, the power from his panels flows into the grid, and he is paid for it. This turns the sun into a second crop. It also gives the farmer a reason to save water, since every unit of power he does not use for pumping can be sold.

Solar pumps alone will not solve the problems of Indian agriculture. Used wisely, though, they can cut costs, free farmers from night-time irrigation and, if the incentives are right, help protect the water on which every farm depends.

stimuli.title: Forests that face the sea
stimuli.content:
Along much of India's coastline, a strip of dense, tangled forest grows where the land meets the sea. Mangroves, trees that can survive in salty water and are flooded twice a day by the tide, were long regarded as wasteland. They were cleared to make room for ports, prawn farms, salt pans and housing, and few people mourned their loss.

That view has changed, largely because of what happens when a cyclone strikes. A belt of mangroves acts like a natural breakwater. Its roots, which rise out of the mud in thick clusters, slow down the waves and trap the sediment the water carries, so that the surge reaching the villages behind is weaker and lower. Studies after major cyclones on the eastern coast found that villages sheltered by healthy mangroves generally suffered less damage than nearby villages whose forests had been cleared, although the size of the effect depended on the width of the forest and the strength of the storm.

Mangroves are also nurseries for the sea. Many fish, crabs and prawns spend their early lives among the roots, where they are protected from larger predators, before moving out into open water. Fishing communities that depend on these catches therefore have a direct stake in the forest's health. In addition, mangrove soils store large amounts of carbon, which would be released into the air if the forests were destroyed.

Restoring mangroves, however, is more difficult than simply planting saplings. Many past planting drives failed because the young trees were placed where the tide did not reach them properly, or because the species chosen did not suit the site. The most successful projects have begun by restoring the natural flow of tidal water and have involved local communities, who know the coast and have a reason to protect what grows on it.

None of this means that mangroves can replace sea walls, cyclone shelters or early-warning systems. It does mean that a forest once dismissed as useless may be among the cheapest and most lasting forms of coastal protection available, provided that it is allowed to grow where nature intended.

stimuli.title: The humble city bus
stimuli.content:
When Indian cities talk about public transport, the conversation usually turns to metro rail. Gleaming new lines are inaugurated with ceremony, and their stations become landmarks. The city bus, by comparison, receives little attention. Yet in most cities buses carry far more passengers than the metro does, and they reach neighbourhoods that no rail line will ever serve.

The neglect shows. In many cities, the number of buses has not kept pace with the population, so waits are long and vehicles are packed at peak hours. Buses share crowded roads with cars and two-wheelers and move at a crawl, which pushes anyone who can afford a vehicle to buy one. More vehicles mean more congestion, which slows the buses further, and the cycle repeats.

Breaking this cycle does not require costly technology. A dedicated lane, painted and enforced, can let a bus move faster than the cars beside it. Reliable timetables, displayed at stops and on phones, allow commuters to plan their journeys instead of waiting anxiously. Low, level boarding helps the elderly, people with disabilities and parents with small children. None of these measures costs more than a fraction of a single kilometre of metro line.

The obstacle is less money than priority. A bus lane takes road space away from private cars, and car owners, though fewer in number than bus passengers, tend to be more influential. Officials who would happily cut the ribbon on a new flyover hesitate to anger motorists by narrowing a road to make room for buses.

Cities that have made buses work, in India and abroad, share one feature: their leaders treated the bus as the backbone of the transport system rather than as a service for those with no other choice. Metro lines have their place, but a city that wants to move most of its people quickly and cheaply will have to start with the vehicle that already carries them.

stimuli.title: When the number becomes the goal
stimuli.content:
A principle familiar to economists and administrators holds that when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. The idea sounds paradoxical, but examples are easy to find. A hospital judged by how quickly it discharges patients may send people home before they are ready, only to see them readmitted a week later. A school rewarded for its pass rate may quietly discourage weaker students from sitting the examination. In each case the number improves while the thing it was meant to reflect stays the same or gets worse.

The reason is not that people are dishonest, though some are. It is that any single figure captures only part of what we care about. A pass rate tells us something about learning, but not everything; a discharge time tells us something about efficiency, but nothing about recovery. As long as nobody is paid or punished according to the figure, it remains a fair, if partial, signal. Once careers depend on it, effort flows towards whatever moves the number most cheaply, and the gap between the figure and the reality it was meant to track widens.

Banking offers its own illustrations. A branch given a target for opening new accounts may open thousands that are never used. A loan officer assessed on the volume of credit disbursed has little reason to dwell on whether the borrowers can repay, since the disbursement is counted today and any default arrives, if at all, years later and on someone else's watch.

None of this is an argument against measurement. An organisation that measures nothing cannot tell success from failure, and the absence of targets usually means that decisions are driven by habit or by whoever speaks loudest. The lesson is rather that numbers should be treated as instruments, not idols. Good practice includes using several indicators at once, so that gaming one shows up as a decline in another; changing targets from time to time before they can be learned and exploited; and, above all, pairing figures with judgement, exercised by people who understand the work well enough to notice when a number has stopped telling the truth.

The most dangerous moment, paradoxically, is when a measure appears to be working best. A figure that rises steadily, year after year, may be a sign of genuine progress, or a sign that people have simply become skilled at producing it.

stimuli.title: The case for keeping cash
stimuli.content:
Over the past decade, digital payments in India have grown at a pace few predicted. A vegetable seller with a printed QR code can now accept money from a stranger in seconds, and many urban consumers go days without touching a banknote. It is tempting to conclude that cash is a relic, and that the sooner it disappears the better. Such a conclusion would be premature.

Cash has qualities that digital money, for all its convenience, does not fully replicate. It works without a network, a battery or a bank account, which matters in a flood, a power failure or a remote village with patchy signal. It settles a transaction finally and instantly: once a note changes hands, there is no server to fail and no payment to reverse. And it offers a degree of privacy that many people value for reasons that have nothing to do with wrongdoing, such as an elderly widow who prefers that her relatives not see every rupee she spends.

The usual objections to cash are real but often overstated. It is true that cash can be used to evade tax and hide illegal income. Yet large-scale evasion increasingly relies on sophisticated devices, such as shell companies and inflated invoices, rather than suitcases of notes, and digital systems carry risks of their own, from fraud to outages. A payment system that depends on a single technology is efficient only for as long as that technology works.

There is also a question of fairness. Those most comfortable with digital payments tend to be young, urban and literate; those most reliant on cash tend to be older, poorer or rural. A shop that refuses notes, or a public service that can be paid for only through an app, shifts the burden of adjustment onto the people least able to bear it.

None of this is an argument for resisting digital payments, whose benefits in speed, record-keeping and reach are considerable. It is an argument for coexistence. A sensible policy would continue to encourage digital transactions while ensuring that cash remains widely accepted, easy to obtain and genuinely usable. The goal should be a society in which people choose digital payments because they are better, not because they have been left with no alternative.

stimuli.title: Gardens on the roof
stimuli.content:
In crowded Indian cities, where every square metre of land is expensive, a quiet green (1) ______ is taking place on rooftops. Families who once used their terraces only for drying clothes are now growing tomatoes, chillies, spinach and herbs in pots, old buckets and grow bags. What began as a hobby for a few retired people has (2) ______ among young professionals, many of whom say that tending plants helps them relax after a long day at a screen.

The benefits go beyond the kitchen. A terrace covered with plants absorbs some of the sun's heat, so the rooms below stay a little cooler in summer. Kitchen waste, instead of being thrown away, can be turned into compost and returned to the soil, which (3) ______ the amount of garbage a household sends to the landfill. Children who help with the watering learn where vegetables come from.

Rooftop farming does have its limits. A roof must be strong enough to bear the weight of wet soil, and water must be drained carefully so that it does not (4) ______ into the building. Beginners often lose their first plants to pests or to too much water. Most gardeners, however, learn quickly, and local groups on social media share tips, seeds and even surplus harvests.

No one expects rooftops to feed a city. But a family that grows even a part of its own vegetables learns how much effort goes into producing food and tends to waste less of it. In that sense, the small garden on the terrace may (5) ______ a lesson far larger than its size.

stimuli.title: Bring your own bottle
stimuli.content:
A walk through any city market shows how much of what we buy comes wrapped in plastic. Shampoo arrives in sachets, rice in printed bags and detergent in pouches that are used once and thrown away. Most of this packaging is (1) ______ to recycle, either because it is made of several layers fused together or because it is too small and dirty to be worth collecting. Much of it ends up in drains, rivers and landfills.

A small but growing number of shops are trying a different approach. Customers bring their own bottles and containers and refill them from large dispensers, paying only for the product, not for the packaging. Some shops weigh the empty container at the counter and (2) ______ its weight from the total, so that nobody pays for glass or steel. Others lend sturdy containers for a small deposit that is returned when the container is brought back.

The model has obvious appeal, but it faces real (3) ______. Shoppers are used to the convenience of picking a packet off the shelf, and carrying containers requires planning. Hygiene rules for loose food are strict, and dispensers must be cleaned regularly. Above all, refill shops are too few to make a difference on their own; a family that has to cross the city to refill a bottle of oil will soon (4) ______ to sachets.

Larger change will probably depend on manufacturers and big retailers. If major brands offered refill stations in ordinary supermarkets, and if rules required companies to take responsibility for the packaging they put on the market, the economics would shift quickly. Until then, the refill shop is less a solution than a (5) ______: proof that buying without throwing away is possible, and a reminder of how far we still have to go.

stimuli.title: Insuring against the sky
stimuli.content:
Every farmer knows that a single failed monsoon can **(1) wipe** out a year's income. Crop insurance is meant to soften such blows, but traditional policies have often disappointed farmers. To settle a claim, an official must visit the field and **(2) ignore** the loss, a process that is slow, costly and open to dispute. By the time the money arrives, the farmer may already have sold his cattle or borrowed at high interest to survive.

Weather-index insurance takes a different route. Instead of measuring the damage in each field, it pays out automatically when an objective index, such as the rainfall recorded at a nearby weather station, crosses an agreed limit. If rainfall during the growing season falls below the threshold, every insured farmer in the area receives a payment, whether or not an inspector has visited. Because no field visits are needed, claims can be settled quickly and administrative costs stay **(3) high**.

The approach has a weakness, which experts call basis risk: the gap between what the index records and what a particular farmer actually suffers. A weather station ten kilometres away may record adequate rain while a farmer's own field remains dry, or a crop may be destroyed by pests in a year when rainfall is perfectly normal. In such cases the farmer suffers a loss but receives nothing, and his trust in insurance is **(4) strengthened**.

Denser networks of weather stations and satellite data can narrow this gap, though they cannot close it entirely. Many specialists therefore see index insurance not as a replacement for traditional cover but as a **(5) substitute** for it: a quick, cheap first payment that keeps a household afloat, while losses that the index misses are handled in other ways.

questions.question_text: Find the value of (6⁴ × 36²) ÷ 216².

solution.concept: Write every term as a power of the same base: aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ and aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ
solution.explanation: 36² = (6²)² = 6⁴ and 216² = (6³)² = 6⁶. So the expression is 6⁴ × 6⁴ ÷ 6⁶ = 6⁴⁺⁴⁻⁶ = 6² = 36.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6, 216 and 1,296 (6¹, 6³ and 6⁴) come from writing 36² as 6³, 6⁵ or 6⁶ by mistake, or from multiplying instead of adding the powers.

solution.concept: Add the two fractions over the common denominator (√11 − √7)(√11 + √7) = 11 − 7
solution.explanation: The common denominator is (√11)² − (√7)² = 4. The numerator is (√11 + √7)² + (√11 − √7)² = 2(11 + 7) = 36. So the value is 36 ÷ 4 = 9.

solution.concept: The cube root of a decimal has one-third as many decimal places; write a mixed number as an improper fraction before taking its root

solution.concept: √(a + b ± 2√ab) = √a ± √b (with √a > √b): find two numbers whose sum is 10 and product is 21
solution.explanation: 7 + 3 = 10 and 7 × 3 = 21, so 10 + 2√21 = (√7 + √3)² and 10 − 2√21 = (√7 − √3)². Since √7 > √3, the roots are √7 + √3 and √7 − √3, and their difference is 2√3.
steps: Need a + b = 10 and ab = 21 ⇒ a = 7, b = 3

solution.explanation: Each term splits as ½(1/n − 1/(n + 2)). Adding from n = 1 to n = 19 (odd n only), the middle terms cancel and the sum is ½(1 − 1/21) = ½ × 20/21 = 10/21.

questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
? ÷ 7.98 × 12.03 ≈ 23.02² − √6399.4 + 16.97 × 4.98

solution.concept: Simplify the right side first, then undo ÷ 8 × 12 (that is, × 1.5)
solution.why_others_wrong: 324, 388 and 420 are each 30 or more away from the exact value (about 354.5).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
√(? + 12.98²) ≈ 22.03 − √48.97

solution.why_others_wrong: 46, 66 and 76 are each at least 8 away from the exact value (about 57.5).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
(8.99³ − 7.02³) ÷ (8.98² + 9.01 × 6.97 + 7.03²) + 55.02% of 399.8 ≈ ?

solution.concept: a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²), so the first fraction is about a − b
solution.explanation: With a ≈ 9 and b ≈ 7, the fraction is (9³ − 7³) ÷ (9² + 9 × 7 + 7²) = 9 − 7 = 2. 55% of 400 = 220. Total ≈ 222.
solution.shortcut: Recognise the identity instead of cubing: the fraction is just 9 − 7.
solution.why_others_wrong: 238 and 206 are 16 away and 191 is 31 away; working out the cubes in full wastes time but gives the same 2.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
?³ + 20.97 × 19.02 ≈ 41.98² − 2.03 × 5.98

solution.concept: Solve for ?³, then find the nearest perfect cube

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
17, 19, 22, 27, 34, 45, ?

solution.concept: The differences are consecutive prime numbers
solution.explanation: The differences are 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, the primes in order. The next prime is 13, so the next term is 45 + 13 = 58.
solution.why_others_wrong: 56 adds 11 again; 60 adds 15 (odd numbers instead of primes); 62 adds 17, skipping 13.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
5, 6, 10, 19, 35, 60, ?

solution.explanation: The differences are 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 = 1², 2², 3², 4², 5². The next difference is 6² = 36, so the next term is 60 + 36 = 96.
solution.why_others_wrong: 92 adds 32; 85 adds 25 again; 97 adds 37.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
3, 7, 16, 35, 74, ?

solution.concept: Each term = previous × 2 + a number that rises by 1 (1, 2, 3, …)
solution.why_others_wrong: 149 adds 1 after doubling (74 × 2 + 1); 151 adds 3; 148 only doubles.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the missing number (?) in the series:
4, 6, 15, 49, ?, 1011

solution.concept: Multiplier rises 1, 2, 3, … and the number added rises 2, 3, 4, …
solution.why_others_wrong: 196 is 49 × 4 with no addition; 205 and 199 do not give 1,011 at the next step.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
8, 12, 24, 48, 88, ?

solution.concept: Two-level differences: the second differences rise by 4
solution.explanation: First differences: 4, 12, 24, 40. Second differences: 8, 12, 16, so the next second difference is 20 and the next first difference is 40 + 20 = 60. The next term is 88 + 60 = 148.
solution.why_others_wrong: 136 adds 48 (differences treated as doubling); 152 adds 64; 144 adds 56.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
1, 8, 9, 64, 25, 216, ?

solution.concept: Alternate positions follow different rules: odd positions are squares, even positions are cubes
solution.explanation: Position n holds n² when n is odd and n³ when n is even: 1², 2³, 3², 4³, 5², 6³. The 7th term is 7² = 49.
solution.why_others_wrong: 343 = 7³ ignores the alternation; 36 = 6² and 125 = 5³ use the wrong base.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
5, 9, 25, 61, 125, ?

solution.concept: The differences are squares of even numbers: 2², 4², 6², …
solution.explanation: The differences are 4, 16, 36, 64 = 2², 4², 6², 8². The next is 10² = 100, so the term is 125 + 100 = 225.
solution.why_others_wrong: 221 adds 96; 189 adds 64 again; 215 adds 90.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
3, 4, 7, 16, 43, ?

solution.explanation: The differences are 1, 3, 9, 27 = 3⁰, 3¹, 3², 3³. The next difference is 81, so the term is 43 + 81 = 124.
solution.shortcut: Equivalently, each term = previous × 3 − 5, 8, 14, …; the difference rule is quicker.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
4, 11, 35, 73, 221, ?

solution.why_others_wrong: 665 applies × 3 + 2 twice in a row; 443 and 447 add 1 or 5 after doubling.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the missing number (?) in the series:
120, ?, 168, 195, 224, 255

solution.concept: Each term is one less than a perfect square
solution.explanation: 120 = 11² − 1, 168 = 13² − 1, 195 = 14² − 1, 224 = 15² − 1 and 255 = 16² − 1, so the missing term is 12² − 1 = 143. The differences 23, 25, 27, 29, 31 confirm it.
solution.why_others_wrong: 144 is 12² itself; 145 and 142 break the odd-number differences.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
2, 3, 11, 38, 102, ?

solution.explanation: The differences are 1, 8, 27, 64 = 1³, 2³, 3³, 4³. The next is 5³ = 125, so the term is 102 + 125 = 227.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
7, 4, 5, 9, 20, 52.5, ?

solution.concept: Multiplier and addend rise together by 0.5: × 0.5 + 0.5, × 1 + 1, × 1.5 + 1.5, …
solution.why_others_wrong: 157.5 is 52.5 × 3 with nothing added; 158 and 162 do not follow either part of the rule.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the missing number (?) in the series:
3, 4, 12, 45, ?, 1005

solution.concept: Each term = previous × n + n², with n = 1, 2, 3, …
solution.why_others_wrong: 184 adds 4 instead of 16; 200 and 192 do not lead to 1,005 (200 × 5 + 25 = 1,025).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
1, 3, 8, 21, 55, ?

solution.explanation: 8 = 3 × 3 − 1, 21 = 3 × 8 − 3, 55 = 3 × 21 − 8, so the next term is 3 × 55 − 21 = 144. (These are alternate Fibonacci numbers.)
solution.shortcut: Differences 2, 5, 13, 34 are themselves alternate Fibonacci numbers; the next difference is 89.
solution.why_others_wrong: 89 is the next difference, not the next term; 134 and 155 use × 3 − 31 or × 3 − 10.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
5, 8, 14, 27, 50, 98, 194

solution.why_others_wrong: 14, 50 and 98 all fit the rule once 27 is corrected to 26.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
980, 958, 914, 846, 760, 650

solution.concept: The terms fall by multiples of 22: 22, 44, 66, …
solution.why_others_wrong: With 848 in place of 846, all the other terms fit; 760 only looks wrong because 846 − 760 = 86.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
4, 9, 25, 49, 81, 169, 289

solution.concept: The terms are squares of consecutive prime numbers
solution.explanation: 4, 9, 25, 49, 169 and 289 are 2², 3², 5², 7², 13² and 17². The fifth term should be 11² = 121; 81 = 9² is the square of a non-prime.
solution.why_others_wrong: 49, 169 and 25 are squares of primes and fit the pattern.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
3, 4, 10, 33, 138, 685, 4,116

solution.concept: Each term = previous × n + n, with n = 1, 2, 3, …
solution.why_others_wrong: 685 looks wrong only if 138 is taken as correct (138 × 5 + 5 = 695); with 136 everything fits.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
2, 7, 27, 109, 427, 1,707, 6,827

solution.why_others_wrong: 427 would be wrong only if 109 were right (109 × 4 − 1 = 435).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Solve the pair of equations given below. Which relation between x and y is true for every pair of roots?
I. x² − 21x + 110 = 0
II. y² − 15y + 54 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Factorise by splitting the middle term; compare the smallest x with the largest y
solution.explanation: x = 10 or 11 and y = 6 or 9. The smallest x (10) is greater than the largest y (9), so x > y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y and x ≤ y come from reading the root signs as negative.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find all the roots of equations I and II, then compare x with y.
I. x² + 11x + 30 = 0
II. y² + 7y + 12 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: With all coefficients positive, both roots are negative
solution.explanation: x = −5 or −6 and y = −3 or −4. The largest x (−5) is smaller than the smallest y (−4), so x < y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y comes from dropping the minus signs (5, 6 against 3, 4).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Equations I and II below are quadratics in x and y. After solving them, mark the relation that always holds.
I. 2x² − 9x + 10 = 0
II. 3y² − 11y + 10 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: A shared root makes the relation non-strict
solution.explanation: x = 2 or 2.5 and y = 2 or 1.67. Every x is at least as large as every y, and x = y = 2 is possible, so x ≥ y.
steps: x = 2, y = 2 gives x = y; all other pairs x > y
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y misses the common root 2.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
One equation below is quadratic and the other linear. Solve both and choose the correct relation between x and y.
I. 2x² + 5x − 12 = 0
II. 5y − 2 = 2y − 6.5

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Solve the linear equation directly; a quadratic root on each side of y means no relation holds
solution.explanation: I: x = 1.5 or −4. II: 3y = −4.5, so y = −1.5. x = 1.5 is greater than y but x = −4 is smaller, so the relation cannot be established.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y uses only the positive root 1.5; x ≤ y uses only −4.
solution.final_answer: Option A: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The equations below have irrational coefficients. Solve them and choose the relation between x and y, if any, that holds for all roots.
I. x² − 7√2x + 24 = 0
II. y² − 6√3y + 24 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Quadratics with surd coefficients: find two roots from their sum and product
solution.explanation: For I, the roots have sum 7√2 and product 24: 3√2 and 4√2 (≈ 4.24 and 5.66). For II, the roots have sum 6√3 and product 24: 2√3 and 4√3 (≈ 3.46 and 6.93). x = 4.24 is above y = 3.46 but below y = 6.93, so no relation holds.
steps: All roots are positive, so compare squares: x² ∈ {18, 32}, y² ∈ {12, 48}
solution.shortcut: Compare the squares of the positive roots: 18, 32 against 12, 48.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y compares only 32 with 48; x ≥ y compares only 18 with 12.
solution.final_answer: Option C: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Both equations below have fractional roots. Determine the roots and select the correct relationship between x and y.
I. 6x² − 7x + 2 = 0
II. 12y² − 7y + 1 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Factorise with a ≠ 1 and compare fractional roots
solution.explanation: x = 1/2 or 2/3 and y = 1/3 or 1/4. The smallest x (0.5) is greater than the largest y (0.33), so x > y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y comes from taking the reciprocals (2, 1.5 against 3, 4) instead of the roots.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The HCF of two numbers is 14 and their LCM is 420. If one of the numbers is 70, what is the other number?

solution.concept: For two numbers, product of the numbers = HCF × LCM
solution.explanation: 70 × other = 14 × 420 = 5,880, so the other number is 5,880 ÷ 70 = 84. Check: HCF(70, 84) = 14 and LCM(70, 84) = 420.
solution.why_others_wrong: 98, 56 and 42 are multiples of 14, but with 70 their LCM is 490, 280 and 210, not 420.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the unit digit of 1! + 2! + 3! + … + 50!?

solution.concept: From 5! onwards every factorial contains 2 × 5, so it ends in 0
solution.explanation: 5!, 6!, …, 50! all end in 0. So only 1! + 2! + 3! + 4! = 1 + 2 + 6 + 24 = 33 decides the unit digit, which is 3.
steps: 5! = 120 and every later factorial is a multiple of 10
solution.why_others_wrong: 0 assumes every term ends in 0; 4 and 9 are the unit digits of 4! and of 1 + 2 + 6 only.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The five-digit number 2a43b, where a and b are digits, is divisible by 72. What is the value of a × b?

solution.concept: 72 = 8 × 9 with 8 and 9 co-prime: test divisibility by 8 (last three digits) and by 9 (digit sum)
solution.explanation: For 8, the last three digits 43b must be a multiple of 8; 432 is the only one, so b = 2. For 9, the digit sum 2 + a + 4 + 3 + 2 = 11 + a must be a multiple of 9, so a = 7. The number is 27,432 = 72 × 381, and a × b = 14.
solution.why_others_wrong: 16, 18 and 12 come from pairs (a, b) that pass only one of the two tests, for example a = 9, b = 2 or b = 6.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the smallest number which, when divided by 8, 12 and 15, leaves remainders 5, 9 and 12 respectively?

solution.concept: If divisor − remainder is the same for every divisor (here 3), the number = k × LCM − that common difference
solution.explanation: 8 − 5 = 12 − 9 = 15 − 12 = 3, so the number is 3 short of a common multiple of 8, 12 and 15. LCM(8, 12, 15) = 120, so the smallest such number is 120 − 3 = 117.
solution.why_others_wrong: 123 adds the 3 instead of subtracting; 237 is the next such number after 117, not the smallest; 113 subtracts 7.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The sum of two positive numbers is 216 and their HCF is 27. How many such pairs of numbers are possible?

solution.concept: Write the numbers as 27a and 27b with a and b co-prime
solution.explanation: 27a + 27b = 216 gives a + b = 8. Co-prime pairs with a < b are (1, 7) and (3, 5); (2, 6) and (4, 4) share a factor. So the pairs are (27, 189) and (81, 135): 2 pairs.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 and 4 include (2, 6) or (4, 4), whose HCF would be 54 or 108; 1 misses (3, 5).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A water tank is 35% full. After 84 litres of water are poured in, it is 56% full. What is the capacity of the tank?

solution.concept: The added water equals the change in the percentage filled
solution.explanation: The 84 litres raise the level from 35% to 56%, that is, by 21% of the capacity. So capacity = 84 ÷ 0.21 = 400 litres.
solution.why_others_wrong: 240 treats 84 litres as 35% of the tank; 150 treats it as 56%; 420 uses 20% instead of 21%.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The price of a television was raised by 25%, then cut by 20% in a sale, and later raised by 10%. What is the overall change in its price?

solution.concept: Successive percentage changes multiply: final = original × (1 + r₁)(1 + r₂)(1 + r₃)
solution.explanation: Multiplying factors: 1.25 × 0.80 × 1.10 = 1.10. The price ends 10% above where it started.
solution.shortcut: A 25% rise followed by a 20% cut cancel exactly (5/4 × 4/5 = 1), leaving only the 10% rise.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15% adds the percentages (25 − 20 + 10); 5% ignores the last rise; 'No change' stops after the first two steps.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A car bought for ₹6,25,000 loses 20% of its value in the first year and 12% of its value at the start of each later year. What is its value after 3 years?

solution.concept: Depreciation on the reducing value: multiply by (1 − rate) year by year
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹3,50,000 subtracts 20% + 12% + 12% = 44% of the original price; ₹4,40,000 is the value after 2 years; ₹3,52,000 applies 20% again in year 3.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Amit's income is 25% more than Bina's. Amit spends 70% of his income and Bina spends 75% of hers. If Amit saves ₹1,500 more than Bina, what is Amit's income?

solution.concept: Express both savings in terms of one income
solution.explanation: Let Bina's income be B. Amit's income is 1.25B and he saves 30% of it, 0.375B. Bina saves 0.25B. The difference 0.125B = 1,500, so B = 12,000 and Amit's income = 15,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹12,000 is Bina's income; ₹18,750 is 1.25 × 15,000; ₹20,000 takes the 1,500 as 7.5% of Amit's income.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In a test, 72% of the candidates passed in Mathematics, 65% passed in English and 18% failed in both. If 495 candidates passed in both subjects, how many candidates took the test?

solution.concept: Sets: passed in at least one = 100% − failed in both; both = M + E − at least one
solution.explanation: 82% passed in at least one subject. So both = 72% + 65% − 82% = 55%. 55% of the total is 495, so the total is 495 ÷ 0.55 = 900.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1,100 takes 495 as 45% of the candidates; 825 takes it as 60%; 990 takes it as 50%.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A town's population of 50,000 grows by 10% every year. At the end of each year, after the growth, 1,000 people move out. What is the population at the end of 2 years?

solution.concept: Apply growth and the fixed outflow year by year; the outflow of year 1 also misses the growth of year 2
solution.why_others_wrong: 58,500 grows 50,000 for both years and subtracts 2,000 at the end, ignoring that the first 1,000 would not have grown; 60,500 ignores migration; 59,500 subtracts only once.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The incomes of A and B are in the ratio 4 : 3 and their expenditures are in the ratio 3 : 2. If each saves ₹6,000 a month, what is A's monthly income?

solution.concept: Income − expenditure = saving; set up the expenditure ratio
solution.explanation: Let the incomes be 4x and 3x. Expenditures are 4x − 6,000 and 3x − 6,000, in the ratio 3 : 2. So 2(4x − 6,000) = 3(3x − 6,000), which gives x = 6,000. A's income = 4x = ₹24,000.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If (3a + 5b) : (3a − 5b) = 7 : 3, what is a : b?

solution.concept: Cross-multiply a proportion: p : q = r : s means ps = qr
solution.shortcut: Componendo-dividendo: 3a : 5b = (7 + 3) : (7 − 3) = 5 : 2, so a : b = 25 : 6.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6 : 25 is inverted; 5 : 3 and 10 : 3 stop at 3a : 5b = 5 : 2 without dividing by 3 and 5 correctly.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: ₹10,800 is divided among A, B and C so that A gets two-thirds of what B and C together get, and B gets one-fourth of what A and C together get. What is B's share?

solution.concept: If X gets p/q of what the others get, X's share = p/(p + q) of the total
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹4,320 is A's (and C's) share; ₹2,700 takes B as one-fourth of the total; ₹1,800 takes it as one-sixth.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Three numbers are in the ratio 2 : 3 : 5 and the sum of their squares is 1,368. What is the largest number?

solution.explanation: (2k)² + (3k)² + (5k)² = 38k² = 1,368, so k² = 36 and k = 6 (the numbers are positive). The numbers are 12, 18 and 30, and the largest is 30.
solution.why_others_wrong: 18 is the middle number; 36 is k², not 5k; 24 corresponds to k = 4.8, whose squares add up to only 875.52.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Ravi is 6 years older than Sunil. Five years ago, Ravi's age was 1.5 times Sunil's age. What is Ravi's present age?

solution.concept: Write both ages five years ago in terms of one unknown
solution.explanation: Let Sunil be S, so Ravi is S + 6. Five years ago: S + 1 = 1.5(S − 5), so S + 1 = 1.5S − 7.5, 0.5S = 8.5 and S = 17. Ravi is 23.
steps: Five years ago: Ravi S + 1, Sunil S − 5
solution.why_others_wrong: 17 is Sunil's age; 29 adds 6 twice; 21 uses S + 6 = 1.5S, ignoring the 5 years.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The sum of the present ages of A and B is 54 years. Eight years from now their ages will be in the ratio 4 : 3. What is B's present age?

solution.concept: Both ages grow by 8, so the future sum is 54 + 16
solution.explanation: In 8 years the sum will be 54 + 16 = 70, split 4 : 3, so A will be 40 and B 30. B's present age = 30 − 8 = 22.
solution.why_others_wrong: 32 is A's present age; 30 is B's age 8 years from now; 24 splits 54 in the ratio 4 : 3 and then subtracts nothing.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average age of a family of five is 28 years. The youngest member is 6 years old. What was the average age of the family just before the youngest member was born?

solution.concept: Go back 6 years: remove the youngest and reduce every other member's age by 6
solution.explanation: Total now = 5 × 28 = 140. Without the youngest, the other four total 134 now. Six years ago each of them was 6 years younger, so their total was 134 − 24 = 110, and the average of the family of four was 110 ÷ 4 = 27.5.
solution.why_others_wrong: 33.5 forgets that the other members were also 6 years younger; 22 subtracts 6 from the average of five; 28 assumes the average does not change.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average of six numbers is 32. Each number is multiplied by 3 and then 5 is added to it. What is the new average?

solution.concept: Multiplying or adding the same amount to every number does the same to the average
solution.explanation: Every number becomes 3x + 5, so the average becomes 3 × 32 + 5 = 101.
solution.why_others_wrong: 96 forgets the + 5; 111 adds 5 before multiplying; 37 only adds 5.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average weight of 20 students is 48 kg. When the teacher's weight is included, the average rises by 1 kg. What is the teacher's weight?

solution.concept: New total − old total = the added weight
solution.explanation: Old total = 20 × 48 = 960 kg. New total = 21 × 49 = 1,029 kg. The teacher weighs 1,029 − 960 = 69 kg.
solution.shortcut: Teacher = new average + (number of students × rise) = 49 + 20 × 1 = 69.
solution.why_others_wrong: 49 kg is the new average; 68 kg adds 20 to the old average; 70 kg adds 21 to the new average.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A grocer mixes 40 kg of rice at ₹52 per kg, 60 kg at ₹45 per kg and some rice at ₹60 per kg. The average cost of the mixture is ₹50 per kg. How many kg of the ₹60 rice did he use?

solution.concept: Weighted average: total cost ÷ total quantity
solution.shortcut: Balance around 50: lot 1 gives +2 × 40 = +80, lot 2 gives −5 × 60 = −300, so the ₹60 rice must give +220 = 10x.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20, 25 and 18 kg leave the mixture's average at about ₹49.8, ₹50.2 and ₹49.7.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average of five consecutive odd numbers is m. If the next three consecutive odd numbers are also included, what is the average of all eight numbers?

solution.concept: Consecutive odd numbers are 2 apart; the average of an evenly spaced list is the middle value
solution.explanation: The five numbers are m − 4, m − 2, m, m + 2, m + 4. The next three are m + 6, m + 8, m + 10. The eight numbers sum to 8m + 24, so the average is m + 3.
solution.shortcut: Eight evenly spaced numbers from m − 4 to m + 10: average = (first + last) ÷ 2 = m + 3.
solution.why_others_wrong: m + 4 averages the first and the eighth wrongly as m and m + 8; m + 6 and m + 5 use the average of the three new numbers alone or forget the first five.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A family's average monthly expenditure was ₹12,000 for the first 5 months of a year, ₹14,500 for the next 4 months and ₹16,000 for the last 3 months. If the family saved ₹26,000 in the whole year, what was its average monthly income?

solution.concept: Annual income = annual expenditure + annual saving; weight each monthly average by its number of months
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹16,333.33 takes the plain average of the three expenditure figures; ₹13,833.33 forgets the savings; ₹15,500 is not supported by any combination of the data.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Kiran buys a used cycle for ₹4,500, spends ₹300 on repairs and sells it for ₹5,400. What is his profit percentage?

solution.concept: Repair costs are part of the cost price
solution.why_others_wrong: 13.33% leaves out the repairs; 11.11% divides by the selling price; 20% takes the profit as ₹900.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The cost price of 15 pens equals the selling price of 12 pens. What is the profit percentage?

solution.concept: Equal amounts of money: compare the number of items
solution.explanation: Let each pen cost ₹1. Then 12 pens sell for ₹15, so the profit on 12 pens is ₹3 on a cost of ₹12, i.e. 25%.
steps: Let CP of 1 pen = 1 ⇒ CP of 15 = 15
solution.why_others_wrong: 20% divides the 3 by 15 instead of 12.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: By selling a watch for ₹2,760, a shopkeeper gains 15%. What would be his gain or loss percentage if he sold it for ₹2,280?

solution.concept: Find the cost price first, then compare the new selling price with it
solution.explanation: CP = 2,760 ÷ 1.15 = 2,400. Selling at 2,280 means a loss of 120, which is 120 ÷ 2,400 = 5% of the cost.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5% gain gets the direction wrong; 4.35% divides 120 by 2,760; 20% divides the drop of 480 by 2,400.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A milkman adds 1 litre of water to every 4 litres of milk and sells the mixture at the cost price of milk. What is his gain percentage?

solution.concept: Water costs nothing, so the gain comes from selling 5 litres for the cost of 4
solution.explanation: 4 litres of milk cost him 4 units. He sells 5 litres of mixture at 1 unit each, getting 5 units. Gain = 1 on 4, which is 25%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20% divides the gain by the 5 litres sold instead of the cost of 4 litres.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The profit made by selling an article for ₹1,860 equals the loss made by selling it for ₹1,340. At what price should it be sold to make a profit of 20%?

solution.concept: If profit at S₁ equals loss at S₂, the cost price is midway: (S₁ + S₂) ÷ 2
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹2,016 starts from 1,680; ₹1,860 already includes a profit of only 16.25%; ₹2,232 adds 20% to 1,860.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The marked price of a sofa is ₹1,500 more than its cost price. When it is sold at a discount of 15%, the shopkeeper makes a profit of ₹600. What is the cost price?

solution.concept: SP = 0.85 × MP and MP = CP + 1,500; profit = SP − CP
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹6,000 is the marked price; ₹4,000 and ₹3,600 give profits of ₹675 and ₹735.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A trader's profit is 25% of his selling price. His cost then rises by 20% while his selling price stays the same. What is his new profit as a percentage of the new cost price?

solution.concept: Profit on SP must be converted to a cost-based figure
solution.explanation: Take SP = 100. Profit = 25, so cost = 75. The new cost = 75 × 1.2 = 90 and the new profit = 10, which is 10 ÷ 90 = 11.11% of the new cost.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5% subtracts 20% from 25%; 10% is profit as a percentage of SP; 8.33% divides 10 by 120.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Rahul sold a scooter to Mohan at a loss of 10%. Mohan spent ₹2,000 on repairs and sold it to Sohan at a profit of 20% on his total cost. If Sohan paid ₹56,400, what did Rahul pay for the scooter?

solution.concept: Work backwards; the repair cost is added to Mohan's cost before his profit
solution.explanation: Mohan's total cost = 56,400 ÷ 1.2 = 47,000. He paid Rahul 47,000 − 2,000 = 45,000, which was 90% of Rahul's cost. So Rahul paid 45,000 ÷ 0.9 = ₹50,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹52,222.22 forgets the repairs; ₹54,444.44 adds them instead of subtracting; ₹47,911.11 takes 20% of the selling price as the profit.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two articles A and B together cost ₹12,000. A is sold at a profit of 15% and B at a loss of 10%, and together they fetch ₹12,480. If A had instead been sold at a loss of 10% and B at a profit of 15%, how much would they have fetched together?

solution.concept: Two unknown costs from the total cost and the total selling price
solution.shortcut: The new total = 2 × 12,000 × 1.025 − 12,480 because each article gets both rates once: 24,600 − 12,480 = 12,120.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹12,480 ignores the swap; ₹11,880 mirrors the gain of 480 into a loss; ₹12,000 assumes the swap cancels.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: An item marked ₹2,500 is sold at a discount of 12%, and the customer gets a further cash discount of ₹50 on the discounted price. How much does the customer pay?

solution.concept: Apply the percentage discount first, then the flat cash discount
solution.explanation: 12% of 2,500 = 300, so the price after discount is 2,200. The cash discount brings it to 2,200 − 50 = ₹2,150.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹2,156 takes the ₹50 off before the 12%; ₹2,200 ignores the cash discount; ₹2,100 takes ₹100 off.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: After two successive discounts of 20% and x%, an article marked at ₹4,000 is sold for ₹2,720. What is x?

solution.concept: Apply the discounts one after the other; the second is on the reduced price
solution.explanation: After 20%: 4,000 × 0.8 = 3,200. The second discount takes it from 3,200 to 2,720, a cut of 480, which is 480 ÷ 3,200 = 15%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 12% takes 480 as a percentage of 4,000; 32% is the single equivalent discount; 18% has no basis.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If a shopkeeper sells an article at a 20% discount, he gains ₹200. If he sells it at a 30% discount, he loses ₹100. What is the cost price of the article?

solution.concept: The extra 10% discount equals the swing from +200 to −100
solution.explanation: Going from 20% to 30% discount lowers the selling price by 10% of MP and changes the result by 200 + 100 = 300. So MP = 3,000. At 20% off, SP = 2,400, and CP = 2,400 − 200 = ₹2,200.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹2,400 is the selling price at 20% off; ₹3,000 is the marked price; ₹2,000 uses a swing of 200 only.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A shop allows successive discounts of 20% and 10% on the marked price of a refrigerator and then adds 18% GST on the discounted price. A customer pays ₹16,992. If the shop's profit is 20% of its cost on the pre-tax price, what is the cost price of the refrigerator?

solution.concept: Strip the tax first, then the profit; the marked price is not needed for the cost
solution.explanation: Pre-tax price = 16,992 ÷ 1.18 = 14,400. This is 120% of the cost, so CP = 14,400 ÷ 1.2 = ₹12,000. (The marked price was 14,400 ÷ 0.72 = ₹20,000.)
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹14,160 removes the 20% profit from the tax-inclusive price; ₹14,400 is the pre-tax selling price; ₹11,520 takes 20% off 14,400 instead of dividing by 1.2.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In how many years will ₹4,800 earn a simple interest of ₹1,512 at 6.3% per annum?

solution.concept: SI = P × R × T ÷ 100, so T = SI × 100 ÷ (P × R)
solution.why_others_wrong: 4.5, 6 and 5.5 years give interest of ₹1,360.80, ₹1,814.40 and ₹1,663.20.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The simple interest on a sum for 5 years at 12% per annum is ₹1,200 less than the sum itself. What is the sum?

solution.concept: Interest for 5 years at 12% is 60% of the principal
solution.explanation: SI = 60% of P, so P − 0.6P = 0.4P = 1,200, which gives P = ₹3,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹2,000 divides 1,200 by 0.6 (taking ₹1,200 as the interest); ₹2,500 and ₹3,600 give differences of ₹1,000 and ₹1,440.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Neha deposits a sum at 8% per annum simple interest. After 2 years she withdraws the interest earned plus ₹5,000 of the principal, and leaves the rest for 3 more years at 10% per annum simple interest. Her total interest over the 5 years is ₹7,700. How much did she deposit?

solution.concept: Split the time into two periods with different principals and rates
solution.explanation: First 2 years: interest = 0.16x. Then the principal is x − 5,000 for 3 years at 10%: interest = 0.3(x − 5,000). So 0.16x + 0.3x − 1,500 = 7,700, giving 0.46x = 9,200 and x = ₹20,000.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What amount will ₹20,000 grow to in 3 years at 5% per annum compound interest, compounded annually?

solution.why_others_wrong: ₹23,000 is the simple-interest amount; ₹22,050 stops at 2 years; ₹24,310.13 runs to 4 years.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: ₹12,500 is invested at compound interest, compounded annually, at 8% for the first year and 10% for the second year. What is the compound interest for the two years?

solution.concept: With different yearly rates, multiply the year factors: P × 1.08 × 1.10
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹2,250 is simple interest (8% + 10% of 12,500); ₹2,351.25 averages the rates to 9% for both years.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A sum amounts to ₹8,820 in 1 year at 10% per annum compound interest, compounded half-yearly. What is the sum?

solution.concept: Half-yearly: rate halves (5%) and periods double (2)
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹8,018.18 divides by 1.10 (annual compounding); ₹7,938 subtracts 10% of 8,820; ₹8,400 divides by 1.05 once.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A sum of money doubles itself in 4 years at compound interest, compounded annually. In how many years will it become 8 times itself at the same rate?

solution.concept: At compound interest, equal time periods multiply the sum by the same factor
solution.explanation: Every 4 years the sum doubles. 8 = 2³, so it needs three doublings: 3 × 4 = 12 years.
solution.why_others_wrong: 16 years treats the growth as linear (8 ÷ 2 × 4); 8 years gives only 4 times.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A loan of ₹31,000 at 10% per annum compound interest, compounded annually, is repaid in two annual instalments, the first at the end of year 1 and the second at the end of year 2. The second instalment is twice the first. What is the first instalment?

solution.concept: Loan = sum of the present values of the instalments
solution.explanation: If the first instalment is x, the present values are x ÷ 1.1 and 2x ÷ 1.21. So x(1.1 + 2) ÷ 1.21 = 31,000, which gives 3.1x = 37,510 and x = ₹12,100. The second instalment is ₹24,200.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹10,333.33 ignores interest (31,000 ÷ 3); ₹11,000 is the present value of the first instalment; ₹12,400 adds simple interest for 2 years and splits it 1 : 2.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Meera invests ₹1,00,000 at 10% per annum compound interest, compounded annually. At the end of each year, just after the interest is added, she withdraws ₹20,000. How much remains in the account just after the third withdrawal?

solution.concept: Add interest, then withdraw, year by year: each withdrawal stops earning interest
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹73,100 subtracts all three withdrawals from the full compound amount, as if the withdrawn money kept earning; ₹70,000 uses simple interest; ₹60,280 withdraws before adding interest.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The simple interest on a sum for 3 years at 12% per annum exceeds the compound interest on the same sum for 3 years at 10% per annum, compounded annually, by ₹290. What is the sum?

solution.concept: Express both interests as fractions of P: SI = 36% of P, CI = (1.1³ − 1) = 33.1% of P
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹14,500 uses 30% for the compound interest (simple interest at 10%); ₹12,000 and ₹9,000 give differences of ₹348 and ₹261.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: ₹16,000 grows to ₹19,448.10 in 2 years at compound interest, compounded half-yearly. What is the rate of interest per annum?

solution.concept: Half-yearly: amount = P(1 + r/200)⁴ over 2 years
solution.explanation: 19,448.10 ÷ 16,000 = 1.21550625 = 1.05⁴. So the half-yearly rate is 5% and the annual rate is 10%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5% is the half-yearly rate, not the annual one; 12% and 20% give amounts of ₹20,199.63 and ₹23,425.60.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A invests ₹35,000 for 8 months and B invests ₹40,000 for 6 months in a business. Out of a profit of ₹26,000, what is A's share?

solution.concept: Profit is shared in the ratio of capital × time
