questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
In the following question, 'A ♠ B' means 'A is greater than B'; 'A ♣ B' means 'A is smaller than B'; 'A ♥ B' means 'A is equal to B'; 'A ♦ B' means 'A is either greater than or equal to B'; 'A ◎ B' means 'A is either smaller than or equal to B'.
Assuming the statements to be true, find which of the conclusions I and II is/are definitely true.

Statements: F ♦ G, G ♥ H, H ♠ I, J ◎ I, J ♣ K

Conclusions:
I. K ♠ H
II. G ♠ J

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: Decoding symbols in a five-statement chain
solution.explanation: Decoded: F ≥ G = H > I ≥ J < K. K and H lie on opposite sides of J, so K > H is not certain. G = H > I ≥ J gives G > J.
steps: Decode: F ≥ G, G = H, H > I, J ≤ I, J < K
Chain: F ≥ G = H > I ≥ J < K
I: K ♠ H means K > H: reversal at J → no relation
II: G ♠ J means G > J: true
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only conclusion II follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: P ≤ Q; R > Q; S ≥ R; T = S; U < T

Conclusions:
I. T > P
II. U > Q

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: Combining five statements into one chain
solution.explanation: Combined: P ≤ Q < R ≤ S = T > U. So T > P. U lies below T on a separate branch, so U and Q cannot be compared.
steps: Chain: P ≤ Q < R ≤ S = T and U < T
I: P ≤ Q < R ≤ S = T → T > P, true
II: Q < … ≤ T > U: reversal at T → no relation
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only conclusion I follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: C ≥ D; D > E; F = E; G ≤ F; H ≥ C

Conclusions:
I. H > G
II. D ≥ F

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: Combining five statements into one chain
solution.explanation: Combined: H ≥ C ≥ D > E = F ≥ G. H > G (one strict sign on the path), and D > E = F gives D > F, which makes D ≥ F true as well.
steps: Chain: H ≥ C ≥ D > E = F ≥ G
II: D > F, so D ≥ F is definitely true
solution.why_others_wrong: A strict relation (D > F) also makes the weaker 'D ≥ F' true.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
In the following question, the symbols π, σ, ω, φ and ψ are used with these meanings:
'P π Q' means 'P is neither smaller than nor equal to Q'; 'P σ Q' means 'P is neither greater than nor equal to Q'; 'P ω Q' means 'P is neither greater than nor smaller than Q'; 'P φ Q' means 'P is not smaller than Q'; 'P ψ Q' means 'P is not greater than Q'.
Assuming the statements to be true, find which of the conclusions I and II is/are definitely true.

Statements: U π V, W φ V, W ψ X, Y ω X, Z σ Y

Conclusions:
I. X π V
II. X ω V

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Either conclusion I or II follows

solution.explanation: Decoded: U > V ≤ W ≤ X = Y > Z. From V to X: V ≤ W ≤ X, so X ≥ V. X > V and X = V are each uncertain, but one of them must hold: either I or II follows.
steps: Decode: U > V, W ≥ V, W ≤ X, Y = X, Z < Y
Chain: U > V ≤ W ≤ X = Y > Z ⇒ X ≥ V
I (X > V) or II (X = V) together = X ≥ V ⇒ Either
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Either' replaces 'Both' (four-option rule).
solution.final_answer: Option D: Either conclusion I or II follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In which of the following expressions are both 'X > Z' and 'W ≥ Y' definitely true?

solution.concept: Testing every expression against both conclusions
solution.explanation: In X ≥ W = Y > V ≥ Z all signs from X to Z point the same way with one strict sign, so X > Z; and W = Y gives W ≥ Y. Every other expression fails one of the two.
steps: X ≥ W = Y > V ≥ Z: X > Z true; W = Y ⇒ W ≥ Y true
X > Y ≥ W = V > Z: X > Z true, but Y ≥ W gives W ≤ Y, so W ≥ Y is not certain
Z ≤ V ≤ Y ≤ W = X: W ≥ Y true, but only X ≥ Z (no strict sign), so X > Z is not certain
X > V ≥ Z = W < Y: X > Z true, but W < Y makes W ≥ Y false
solution.final_answer: Option B: X ≥ W = Y > V ≥ Z

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: J > K ≥ L; M ≤ L; N > M; O = K

Which of the following conclusions is definitely true?

solution.concept: Checking each option against the combined chain
solution.explanation: Combined: J > K ≥ L ≥ M < N, with O = K. From J down to M every sign points the same way and one is strict, so J > M. N lies above M on a separate branch, so N cannot be compared with L or K; and O = K ≥ L gives only O ≥ L.
steps: Chain: J > K ≥ L ≥ M < N; O = K
J > M: J > K ≥ L ≥ M → true
N > L and N ≥ K: N and L/K are joined only through M, where the direction turns → not definite
O > L: O = K ≥ L gives only O ≥ L → not definite

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Introducing a boy, Sunita said, "His father is the only son of my mother." How is Sunita related to the boy?

solution.concept: Collapsing 'the only son of my mother'
solution.explanation: Sunita's mother's only son is Sunita's brother. The boy's father is therefore Sunita's brother, so Sunita is the boy's father's sister: his aunt.
steps: My mother's only son = Sunita's brother
solution.why_others_wrong: Mother would need Sunita to be the boy's parent, but his father is her brother; sister would need the same father for both.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: P is the wife of Q. R is the father of Q. S is the only daughter of R. How is S related to P?

solution.explanation: R is Q's father and S is R's daughter, so S is Q's sister. P is Q's wife, so S is P's husband's sister: her sister-in-law.
steps: R is Q's father; S is R's daughter ⇒ S is Q's sister
solution.why_others_wrong: Mother-in-law would be R's wife; S is not P's own sister or daughter.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Tanvi's father is the only son of Rakesh's father. Rakesh is a man. How is Rakesh related to Tanvi?

solution.concept: 'The only son of my father' is the man himself
solution.explanation: Rakesh is a son of his own father, and his father has only one son, so that only son is Rakesh. Tanvi's father is therefore Rakesh.
steps: 'Only son' ⇒ the only son is Rakesh
solution.why_others_wrong: Uncle would need Rakesh's father to have a second son; grandfather and brother ignore the word 'only'.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If 'P ↑ Q → R ↓ S', how is P related to S?

solution.concept: Two parents of the same child
solution.explanation: P is Q's father; Q is R's sister, so P is R's father too. R is S's daughter, so S is R's other parent. Since P is the father, S is the mother, and P is S's husband.
steps: P ↑ Q: P is Q's father
Q → R: Q and R are sisters ⇒ P is R's father
R ↓ S: S is R's parent ⇒ S is the mother
solution.why_others_wrong: Father would make S P's child, but S is a parent of P's daughter R.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If 'J ↔ K ← L → M', how is J related to M?

solution.concept: Mother's sibling's relation to the child
solution.explanation: J is K's son and K is L's husband, so L is J's mother. L is M's sister, so M is J's mother's sibling, and J is M's nephew.
steps: J ↔ K: J is K's son
K ← L: K is L's husband ⇒ L is J's mother
L → M: L is M's sister
J = son of M's sister ⇒ nephew
solution.why_others_wrong: Cousin is J's relation to M's children; brother-in-law is K's relation to M.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If 'U → V ↑ W ↔ X', how is U related to X?

solution.concept: The other parent of a child is the father's wife
solution.explanation: U is V's sister; V is W's father; W is X's son, so X is W's other parent, i.e. V's wife. U is the sister of X's husband: X's sister-in-law.
steps: U → V: U is V's sister
V ↑ W: V is W's father
W ↔ X: X is W's parent ⇒ X is V's wife
solution.why_others_wrong: Aunt is U's relation to W, not to X; mother-in-law would be V's mother.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which of the following expressions means that A is the grandfather of C?

solution.explanation: 'A ↑ B ↑ C': A is B's father and B is C's father, so A is C's grandfather. In 'A ↑ B ↓ C', C is the mother of A's daughter (A's wife); in 'A ↔ B ↑ C', A and C are both B's sons (brothers); in 'A ← B ↓ C', A is the husband of C's daughter (son-in-law).
steps: A ↑ B ↑ C: father of father ⇒ grandfather
A ↑ B ↓ C ⇒ A is C's husband
A ↔ B ↑ C ⇒ A is C's brother
A ← B ↓ C ⇒ A is C's son-in-law

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is Anjali's profession?

solution.explanation: Lawyer, Teacher (oldest generation), Doctor (Savita's daughter-in-law), Engineer (the father), Banker and Student (the two children) are all taken by others, so Anjali is the Pilot.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How is the Banker related to the Engineer?

solution.explanation: The Banker is Kriti and the Engineer is Vikas, her father: she is his daughter.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How is the Lawyer related to the Student?

solution.explanation: The Lawyer is Ramesh and the Student is Dhruv, the son of Ramesh's son Vikas: Ramesh is his grandfather.
steps: Dhruv's father Vikas is Ramesh's son ⇒ grandfather

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How is the Pilot related to the Doctor?

solution.explanation: The Pilot is Anjali and the Doctor is Pooja; Anjali is the sister of Pooja's husband Vikas, so she is Pooja's sister-in-law.
steps: Anjali is Vikas's sister; Vikas is Pooja's husband

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

solution.explanation: 'M ! N ^ Q': M is N's mother and N is Q's husband, so M is the mother of Q's husband: Q's mother-in-law. In 'M ! N ? Q', N is the son of M and of Q, so M is Q's wife. In 'M ~ N ! Q', M is the sister of Q's mother (aunt). In 'M = N ^ Q', M is the daughter of N and of N's wife Q.
steps: M ! N ^ Q ⇒ M is Q's husband's mother ⇒ mother-in-law
M ! N ? Q ⇒ M and Q are N's parents ⇒ M is Q's wife
M ~ N ! Q ⇒ M is Q's aunt
M = N ^ Q ⇒ M is Q's daughter

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
A family has seven members: Ganga, Harish, Indu, Jatin, Kamal, Leela and Manya.
- Ganga is the wife of Harish, and Jatin is their only child.
- Jatin is married to Indu.
- Kamal is the only son of Indu.
- Leela's husband is the only grandson of Harish.
- Manya is the daughter of Leela.

How is Manya related to Ganga?

solution.explanation: Jatin is Ganga's son. Kamal is the son of Indu, Jatin's wife, so Kamal is Ganga's grandson; Harish has no other child, so Kamal is his only grandson and Leela is Kamal's wife. Manya is Kamal's daughter: three generations below Ganga, i.e. her great-granddaughter.
steps: Generation 2: their only child Jatin (+ Indu)
Generation 3: Kamal, son of Jatin and Indu = Harish's only grandson (+ Leela)
Generation 4: Manya, daughter of Kamal and Leela ⇒ great-granddaughter of Ganga
solution.why_others_wrong: Granddaughter skips a generation; grandniece needs a sibling link that does not exist; great-grandmother reverses the relation.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Rakesh walks 9 m towards the south. He then turns left and walks 12 m, and then turns left again and walks 4 m. How far is he now from his starting point, and in which direction?

solution.explanation: Left from south is east, and left from east is north. He ends 12 m east and 9 − 4 = 5 m south of the start: √(144 + 25) = 13 m, towards the south-east.
solution.why_others_wrong: South-West mixes up the first left turn; 25 m adds the legs; North-East ignores that he is still south of the start.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: One morning after sunrise, Vivek was walking along a straight road and his shadow fell exactly to his left. He then turned right twice, 90° each time, and kept walking. Where does his shadow fall now?

solution.explanation: In the morning the sun is in the east, so shadows point west. A shadow on his left means west is his left, so he was facing north. Two right turns make him face south, and for a person facing south the west is on the right.
steps: Morning: sun in the east ⇒ shadow towards the west
West on his left ⇒ facing north
Two right turns: north → east → south
Facing south, west is to the right ⇒ shadow to his right
solution.why_others_wrong: 'To his left' ignores the turns; a shadow falls behind or in front only when facing east or west.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: A robot starts at point O facing north. It moves 1 m forward, turns right and moves 2 m, turns right and moves 3 m, and so on: before every move after the first it turns right, and each move is 1 m longer than the one before. It stops after its tenth move, of 10 m. How far is it from O, and in which direction?

solution.concept: A square spiral: add the moves in each direction
solution.explanation: The moves go north, east, south, west in turn. North: 1 + 5 + 9 = 15; south: 3 + 7 = 10; east: 2 + 6 + 10 = 18; west: 4 + 8 = 12. Net: 5 m north and 6 m east, so the distance is √(25 + 36) = √61 m, towards the north-east.
steps: Directions repeat N, E, S, W: moves 1, 5, 9 north; 2, 6, 10 east; 3, 7 south; 4, 8 west
solution.why_others_wrong: North-West swaps east and west; 11 m adds the two net components; 5 m, East ignores the northward component and the eastward sum.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code language, FOREST is written as ULIVHG. How is MARKET written in that code language?

solution.explanation: F (6) ↔ U (21), O (15) ↔ L (12), R ↔ I, E ↔ V, S ↔ H, T ↔ G: each letter is replaced by its opposite, the letter whose position adds up with it to 27. MARKET: M ↔ N, A ↔ Z, R ↔ I, K ↔ P, E ↔ V, T ↔ G.
steps: MARKET → N Z I P V G
solution.why_others_wrong: NZIQVG takes K as Q; LZIPVF and OBJPWH shift some letters instead of using opposites.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, CANDLE is written as FMEOBD. How is BUTTER written in that code?

solution.concept: Reverse the word, then move each letter one step forward
solution.explanation: CANDLE reversed is ELDNAC; moving each letter one step forward gives FMEOBD. BUTTER reversed is RETTUB, and one step forward gives SFUUVC.
solution.why_others_wrong: CVUUFS shifts without reversing; QDSSTA reverses and shifts backwards; SFUUVD gets the last letter wrong.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, SMILE is written as TOLPJ. How is BRAVE written in that code?

solution.concept: Each letter moves forward by its own position number
solution.explanation: S + 1 = T, M + 2 = O, I + 3 = L, L + 4 = P, E + 5 = J. BRAVE: B + 1 = C, R + 2 = T, A + 3 = D, V + 4 = Z, E + 5 = J → CTDZJ.
solution.why_others_wrong: CSBWF moves every letter by 1; CTDZK adds 6 to the last letter; DTDZJ adds 2 to the first.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, BAG is written as 10 and DIG is written as 20. How is HIDE written in that code?

solution.why_others_wrong: 22 leaves out D (4); 30 adds the number of letters; 104 multiplies the sum by the number of letters.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the code for 'crops'?

solution.concept: One common word, one common code
solution.explanation: 'crops' appears in sentences 2 and 3, whose only common code is ne.
steps: Sentence 2: zi pe ra ne; sentence 3: ne mo fa

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which word is coded as 'bo'?

solution.explanation: Sentence 4 is 'care for green fields' = 'fa ka lu bo'. care = fa (shared with sentence 3) and green and fields take ka and lu (shared with sentence 1), so bo = for.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the code for 'need rain'?

solution.explanation: need appears in sentences 1 and 3 (common code mo), and rain in sentences 1 and 2 (common code zi).
steps: need: {ka mo zi lu} ∩ {ne mo fa} = mo
rain: {ka mo zi lu} ∩ {zi pe ra ne} = zi

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, TRAIN is written as SQBJM and BUS is written as AVR. How is METRO written in that code?

solution.concept: Vowels and consonants move in opposite directions
solution.explanation: TRAIN: T−1 = S, R−1 = Q, A+1 = B, I+1 = J, N−1 = M. BUS: B−1 = A, U+1 = V, S−1 = R. Each vowel moves one step forward and each consonant one step back. METRO: M → L, E → F, T → S, R → Q, O → P.
steps: Check TRAIN and BUS: vowels +1, consonants −1
METRO: M−1 L, E+1 F, T−1 S, R−1 Q, O+1 P
solution.why_others_wrong: LDSQN moves every letter back; NFUSP moves every letter forward; LFSQN moves the final O back instead of forward.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, MARKET is written as SBNUFL. How is PLANET written in that code?

solution.concept: Reverse each half, then move each letter one step forward
solution.explanation: MARKET → halves MAR | KET → reversed RAM | TEK → each letter +1 → SBN | UFL. PLANET → PLA | NET → ALP | TEN → +1 → BMQUFO.
steps: Check: MAR KET → RAM TEK → SBN UFL
solution.why_others_wrong: UFOBMQ reverses the whole word; QMBOFU only shifts; BMQOFU leaves the second half unreversed.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, 4721 is written as 4507 and 3916 is written as 9426. How is 5803 written in that code?

solution.concept: Add 3 to each digit (keeping the units digit), then reverse
solution.why_others_wrong: 8136 skips the reversal; 3081 reverses without adding; 6138 reverses only part of the number.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the code for 'MARGIN'?

solution.explanation: MARGIN has 6 letters (even), so the halves MAR and GIN are interchanged: GINMAR. Its vowels I and A become J and B: GJNMBR.
solution.why_others_wrong: MBRGJN skips the swap; GINMAR skips Step 2; HJONBS shifts consonants too.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the code for 'PLANT'?

solution.explanation: PLANT has 5 letters (odd), so the middle letter A is replaced by 5: PL5NT. No vowel is left, so Step 2 changes nothing.
solution.why_others_wrong: PLBNT applies only Step 2 to A; NTAPL swaps halves (that is for even lengths); PL5OT shifts N.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the code for 'OBTAINED'?

solution.explanation: OBTAINED has 8 letters, so OBTA and INED are interchanged: INEDOBTA. The vowels I, E, O, A become J, F, P, B: JNFDPBTB.
steps: Vowels: I → J, E → F, O → P, A → B (twice)
solution.why_others_wrong: PBTBJNFD skips the swap; INEDOBTA skips Step 2; JNFDPBUB also shifts the consonant T.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, CODE is written as GRFF and HAND is written as LDPE. How is LAMP written in that code?

solution.concept: Shift by the position counted from the right end
solution.explanation: CODE: C+4 = G, O+3 = R, D+2 = F, E+1 = F. HAND: H+4 = L, A+3 = D, N+2 = P, D+1 = E. Each letter moves forward by its position counted from the right end. LAMP: L+4 = P, A+3 = D, M+2 = O, P+1 = Q.
steps: LAMP: L+4 P, A+3 D, M+2 O, P+1 Q
solution.why_others_wrong: MCPT counts positions from the left (+1, +2, +3, +4); PDPQ adds 3 to M; QDOP swaps the end letters.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, ACE is written as 22 and BAD is written as 16. Using the same rule, how is CAGE written?

solution.concept: Position value × place in the word, added up
solution.explanation: ACE: 1×1 + 3×2 + 5×3 = 1 + 6 + 15 = 22. BAD: 2×1 + 1×2 + 4×3 = 2 + 2 + 12 = 16. Each letter's alphabet position is multiplied by its place in the word and the products are added. CAGE: 3×1 + 1×2 + 7×3 + 5×4 = 3 + 2 + 21 + 20 = 46.
steps: Check ACE = 22 and BAD = 16 (plain sums would be 9 and 7)
solution.why_others_wrong: 16 is the plain sum of positions; 34 multiplies by the places counted from the right end; 64 multiplies the sum by the number of letters.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Study the following arrangement of letters, numbers and symbols and answer the question.

T 6 # B 9 E 3 @ K 7 W % 2 U 8

Which element is 4th to the left of the 10th element from the left end?

solution.concept: Moving left from a counted position
solution.explanation: The 10th element from the left is 7; four places to its left is the 6th element, E.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How many letters in the arrangement are immediately preceded by a number and immediately followed by a symbol?

solution.explanation: Letters with a number before and a symbol after: 8 A @, 4 R & — 2 in all.
steps: Scan each letter: left neighbour a number? right neighbour a symbol?

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If all the numbers in the arrangement are removed, which element will be 7th from the right end?

solution.explanation: Without numbers the arrangement is M # J A @ Q W E % K $ U R & Y. Counting from the right, the 7th element is %.
steps: New arrangement: M # J A @ Q W E % K $ U R & Y

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which element is 5th to the left of the 12th element from the left end?

solution.concept: Moving left from a counted position
solution.explanation: The 12th element from the left is E; five places to its left is the 7th element, @.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How many vowels in the arrangement are immediately followed by a consonant?

solution.explanation: The vowels are A, E and U. A is followed by @, E by %, U by 4: none is followed by a consonant.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If the first twelve elements are written in reverse order, which element will be 6th to the right of the 8th element from the left end?

solution.explanation: After reversing the first twelve: # 7 D N 3 ★ I H 8 © R 5 O 4 G £ 9 S 2 L ¥ A 6 P. The 8th element is H; six places to its right is the 14th, 4.
steps: New order: # 7 D N 3 ★ I H 8 © R 5 O 4 G £ 9 S 2 L ¥ A 6 P

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How many symbols in the arrangement are immediately preceded by a letter and immediately followed by a number?

solution.explanation: Matches: R © 8, I ★ 3, G £ 9 — 3 in all.
steps: Letter before and number after: R © 8, I ★ 3, G £ 9

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which element is exactly midway between the 5th element from the left end and the 6th element from the right end?

solution.concept: Converting a right-end position before taking the midpoint
solution.explanation: The 5th from the left is position 5 (H); the 6th from the right is position 19 (2). Midway: position 12, #.
steps: 6th from the right = 24 − 6 + 1 = 19th from the left

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Study the following arrangement of letters, numbers and symbols and answer the question.

8 F @ 3 K U 6 % T 1 Z $ 4 E 7 B # 9 M 2 & O 5 V

How many even numbers in the arrangement have at least one symbol as an immediate neighbour?

solution.concept: Checking both neighbours of each even number
solution.explanation: Even numbers and their neighbours: 8 (—, F); 6 (U, %); 4 ($, E); 2 (M, &). With a symbol beside: 3.
steps: Check left and right neighbours for a symbol

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Study the following arrangement of letters, numbers and symbols and answer the question.

8 F @ 3 K U 6 % T 1 Z $ 4 E 7 B # 9 M 2 & O 5 V

If all the vowels are removed from the arrangement, which element will be 4th to the left of the 9th element from the left end?

solution.explanation: Without the vowels U, E and O: 8 F @ 3 K 6 % T 1 Z $ 4 7 B # 9 M 2 & 5 V. The 9th element is 1; four places to its left is the 5th, K.
steps: New arrangement: 8 F @ 3 K 6 % T 1 Z $ 4 7 B # 9 M 2 & 5 V

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In the word 'CHAMPION', the 1st and 5th letters are interchanged, and so are the 2nd and 6th, the 3rd and 7th, and the 4th and 8th letters. Which letter will then be 3rd from the right end?

solution.concept: Interchanging positions k and k + 4 swaps the two halves
solution.explanation: Swapping 1↔5, 2↔6, 3↔7, 4↔8 exchanges the halves CHAM and PION: PIONCHAM. From the right: M, A, H.
solution.why_others_wrong: A is 2nd from the right; C is 5th from the left; O is the 3rd from the left.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If 2 is added to the last digit of each number, in how many of the new numbers will the last digit be greater than the first digit?

solution.explanation: New numbers: 647 → 649, 382 → 384, 915 → 917, 274 → 276, 536 → 538. Last digit greater than first: 649, 384, 276, 538. Count 4.
steps: Compare last digit with first digit

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If the numbers are arranged in descending order, which number will be third from the left?

solution.explanation: Descending: 915, 647, 536, 382, 274. Third from the left: 536.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a row of girls facing north, Nisha is 9th from the left end. When she moves 5 places to her right, she becomes 14th from the right end. How many girls are there in the row?

solution.explanation: After moving 5 places right, Nisha is 9 + 5 = 14th from the left and 14th from the right, so the row has 14 + 14 − 1 = 27 girls.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

solution.concept: Removing students above a person does not change the count below
solution.explanation: Below Ravi there were 45 − 16 = 29 students, and none of them was removed. So he is still 30th from the bottom (his rank from the top changes to 11th).
solution.why_others_wrong: 25th wrongly subtracts the five removed students from the bottom count; 35th and 26th mix up the ends.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

solution.concept: Midpoint, then total from both ends
solution.explanation: Charu is midway between the 15th and 23rd places: (15 + 23) ÷ 2 = 19th from the front. With 18th from the back, the queue has 19 + 18 − 1 = 36 people.
solution.why_others_wrong: 37 forgets to subtract Charu once; 35 subtracts twice; 41 uses Bhola's place.

II. Sonu's present age is half of Ramu's present age.

options.text: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not sufficient
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not sufficient
Statements I and II together are not sufficient
Both statements I and II together are necessary

solution.concept: Data sufficiency: test each statement alone, then together
solution.explanation: I alone or II alone fits many pairs of ages. Together: R = S + 4 and R = 2S give S = 4 and R = 8.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

II. T is shorter than Q.

options.text: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not sufficient
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not sufficient
Statements I and II together are not sufficient
Both statements I and II together are necessary

solution.concept: Data sufficiency: test each statement alone, then together
solution.explanation: I leaves T unplaced (T could be taller than S). II alone places only T and Q. Together, T is below Q, which is below P and S, so S is the tallest.
steps: I: S > P > Q, R; T unknown: not sufficient
II: T < Q only: not sufficient
I + II: T < Q < P < S ⇒ S is the tallest
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both statements I and II together are necessary

options.text: Only statements I and II together are sufficient
Only statements II and III together are sufficient
All three statements I, II and III together are necessary
Even all three statements together are not sufficient

solution.explanation: I + II: T > R > P, and P is above Q and S, so P is third. II + III: T > R > P and S > Q, but S may be above P. I + III: P > S > Q, but T and R are unplaced. So only I and II together are sufficient.

II + III: P vs S unknown: not sufficient
I + III: T and R unplaced: not sufficient

options.text: Only statements I and II together are sufficient
All three statements I, II and III together are necessary
Any two of the three statements together are sufficient
Even all three statements together are not sufficient

solution.explanation: No statement alone fixes gold (II does not even contain it). I + II: coin = ki, so gold = pa. I + III: the only common code of the two sentences containing gold is pa. II + III: silver = lo, so gold = pa. Any two statements are sufficient.
steps: I alone: gold ∈ {pa, ki}; III alone: gold ∈ {lo, pa}; II alone: no gold
I + II: coin = ki ⇒ gold = pa
I + III: common code pa ⇒ gold = pa
II + III: silver = lo ⇒ gold = pa
solution.final_answer: Option C: Any two of the three statements together are sufficient

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two assumptions. An assumption is something supposed or taken for granted by the person making the statement. Decide which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement.

Statement: Announcement at a railway station: "Passengers are advised to keep their luggage with them at all times."

Assumptions:
I. Luggage left unattended at the station may get lost or stolen.
II. Most passengers travel without any luggage.

options.text: Neither I nor II is implicit
Both I and II are implicit

solution.concept: Implicit assumption: what the speaker must take for granted
solution.explanation: The advice makes sense only if leaving luggage unattended carries a risk such as loss or theft, so I is implicit. The announcement is addressed to passengers who do carry luggage; it assumes nothing about most passengers travelling without it (II).
steps: Why advise keeping luggage close? Because unattended luggage is at risk ⇒ I implicit
II contradicts the purpose of the announcement ⇒ not implicit
solution.why_others_wrong: Both and Only II accept II, which the announcement does not need (and which runs against it).
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only assumption I is implicit

Assumptions:

options.text: Neither I nor II is implicit
Both I and II are implicit

solution.concept: Implicit assumption: what the speaker must take for granted
solution.explanation: Choosing the time 'just before the monsoon' assumes that this timing helps the saplings survive (I). Deciding to plant saplings along the main roads assumes that saplings can be planted there (II); otherwise the plan could not be carried out.
steps: The timing was chosen deliberately ⇒ it is believed to help survival: I implicit
A plan to plant along the main roads presumes that planting there is possible: II implicit
solution.why_others_wrong: Only I or Only II misses one of the two premises the decision rests on; Neither ignores both.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both I and II are implicit
